query: Which case came first, Craig v. Boren or United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc.?

pipeline_result.response: The case that came first is United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc., which was a landmark Supreme Court antitrust case in 1948. The case involved the decision of the United States Supreme Court to strike down the existing distribution scheme for movie studios and their exclusive deals with theaters on which films were shown.
retrieved_context: United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc.: United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc., 334 US 131 (1948) (also known as the Hollywood Antitrust Case of 1948, the Paramount Case, the Paramount Decision or the Paramount Decree) was a landmark United States Supreme Court antitrust case that decided the fate of movie studios owning their own theatres and holding exclusivity rights on which theatres would show their films.  It would also change the way Hollywood movies were produced, distributed, and exhibited.  The Court held in this case that the existing distribution scheme was in violation of the antitrust laws of the United States, which prohibit certain exclusive dealing arrangements.

Craig v. Boren: Craig v. Boren, 429 U.S. 190 (1976) , was the first case in which a majority of the United States Supreme Court determined that statutory or administrative sex classifications were subject to intermediate scrutiny under the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.
